posts.title: No jurisdiction becomes Crypto Valley by accident.
posts.author: Goldblum and Partners
posts.snippet:
No jurisdiction becomes Crypto Valley by accident.
Zug wrote a playbook other regulators are still copying.

The Ethereum Foundation settled in Zug in 2014, before most supervisors had an opinion on token sales. Twelve years later, more than 1,000 blockchain companies operate in and around the canton. The interesting part is not the headcount. It is how predictable the legal mechanics behind it have become.

What a serious Zug relocation memo covers 📋

🔷 Classification before structure. Eidgenössische Finanzmarktaufsicht FINMA's guidelines of February 2018 sort tokens into payment, utility and asset categories, and that classification drives everything downstream: prospectus duties, licensing tier, AML scope. Founders who skip this step usually redo their structure later.

🔷 Formation mechanics are standard corporate law. An AG needs CHF 100'000 in share capital, a GmbH CHF 20'000, and Zug commercial register practice has accepted crypto assets as contributions in kind. There is no special "crypto company" form, and none is needed.

🔷 The AML floor arrives before the first client. Exchange or custody services mean financial intermediary status, which requires SRO membership
posts.reason: Detailed Swiss token classification and formation mechanics from a trusted source, valuable for deep-tech and crypto founders evaluating jurisdiction strategy and token structure decisions.

comments.text: The FINMA 2018 guidelines are still doing a lot of work seven years on — the payment/utility/asset split drives not just prospectus and AML scope in Switzerland but is the same starting question we ask under MiCAR, even though the EU's three categories (utility, e-money, asset-referenced) don't map cleanly onto FINMA's.
Does the commercial register in Zug still accept crypto assets as contributions in kind case by case, or has practice settled into something closer to a standard valuation methodology now?

We get the same conversation from clients weighing Zug against an EU CASP authorisation — the corporate mechanics are genuinely simple, it's the AML/SRO membership timeline that ends up being the long pole, same as MiCA's CASP process here.

posts.title: Ninety-nine crypto projects sit on RootData's running list of this year's casualties and it is only July. Five of them are exchanges. Why they actually died has less to do with reg
posts.author: Dmitry Zamkovoy, FRM
posts.snippet:
Ninety-nine crypto projects sit on RootData's running list of this year's casualties and it is only July. Five of them are exchanges. Why they actually died has less to do with regulation, or with the offshore-to-onshore drift, than the surface suggests.

On 1 July the MiCA transitional period ended and three exchanges lost EU access at once. Binance had withdrawn its Greek application a week earlier, after a Reuters report it disputed that the regulator was preparing to reject it; it suspended EU services, kept withdrawals open and is now applying in France. MEXC, unlicensed and absent from the ESMA register, told EEA users in June its service was changing. AscendEX ceased operations altogether, citing the missing authorisation and a liquidity deal whose counterparty failed to deliver.

Not one of the three held a licence. Yet as things stand one is fine, another is inconvenienced and the third may not pay its clients back. Whatever separated them, it was not the paper.

Now consider two others. BitMEX dominated crypto derivatives through the late 2010s, never lost a client dollar to a hack, and its assets exceeded its liabilities at the end. Its parent shopped it from February 2025 and, eighteen months on, found no buyer; it shuts on 23 September. Hyperliquid, licensed nowhere either, reached roughly 9% of global perps open interest in early July across centralised and decentralised venues. The former had every credential this industry recognises and could not be given away; the latter has none and is taking share.

It shows in what people pay. SBI agreed in June to buy Bitbank for about $289 million; Polygon Labs paid over $250 million in January for Coinme and Sequence, mainly for US money-transmitter licences and fifty thousand retail cash locations. Brokers, meanwhile, advertise clean transitional CASP entities in Lithuania, Cyprus and Malta at €200,000 to €600,000. Nobody pays nine figures for an authorisation that trades in six.

What separated these cases was simpler than the regulatory story allows. Binance could drop Greece and file in France. Bybit saw the cliff coming and had an Austrian entity authorised in May 2025. AscendEX had nowhere to go. BitMEX had a famous name and no client whose departure a buyer feared losing. BitMart, nine years old and reporting $1.6 billion in daily volume, up 51% on the previous period, concluded there was no future worth funding. Volume did not save it, any more than longevity or a recognisable brand saved the others; an edge is a reason a client would refuse to trade anywhere else.

Flow is concentrating toward venues that can answer the question: why here? Some are offshore, built on scale and product velocity that regulation was never going to grant. Others are regulated and have built customers and distribution on top of the licence. That, not the licence, is the part a buyer pays for. 

What they share is not jurisdiction or size but a client who can name the reason they stay.

posts.title: Art 50 AI Act macht KI-Transparenz auch zur Beschaffungsfrage
posts.author: Schiefer Rechtsanwälte GmbH
posts.snippet:
Art 50 AI Act macht KI-Transparenz auch zur Beschaffungsfrage

Art 50 AI Act verpflichtet nicht pauschal zur sichtbaren Kennzeichnung jedes KI-generierten Inhalts, sondern bringt mit 2.8.2026 weitere Pflichten rund um Transparenz, KI-Interaktionen und bestimmte KI-generierte Inhalte. Zu beachten ist, dass mit der am 24.7.2025 veröffentlichten Digital-Omnibus-VO (VO (EU) 2026/1744) kurzfristig eine praxisrelevante Übergangsfrist bis 2.12.2026 für Anbieter von KI-Systemen iSd Art 50 Abs 2 AI Act geschaffen wurde.

Für öffentliche Auftraggeber ist das in zweifacher Hinsicht relevant:

Erstens können Behörden selbst „Betreiber“ im Sinne des AI Act sein. Das betrifft etwa Bürger-Chatbots, virtuelle Assistenten, KI-generierte Informationskampagnen oder Veröffentlichungen zu Verwaltung, Gesundheit, Umwelt und anderen öffentlichen Angelegenheiten.

Zweitens muss #Compliance bereits in der #Beschaffung mitgedacht werden. In Ausschreibungen für KI-Systeme sollten daher insbesondere vorgesehen werden:

•	Funktionen zur maschinenlesbaren Markierung und zur sichtbaren Offenlegung,
•	barrierefreie Hinweise spätestens bei der ersten Interaktion oder Wahrnehmung,
•	Nachweise, Test- und Abnahmekriterien für die Einhaltung des Art. 50,
•	klare Verantwortlichkeiten zwischen Anbieter und öffentlichem Auftraggeber,
•	Aktualisierungs-, Dokumentations- und Mängelbehebungspflichten während der Vertragslaufzeit.

Art-50-Compliance sollte daher nicht erst nach Zuschlagserteilung geprüft, sondern als funktionale Anforderung (§ 104 BVergG 2018) und Vertragsbestandteil festgelegt werden.

Die entscheidende Frage lautet daher nicht nur: „Welches KI-System beschaffen wir?“

Sondern auch: „Ermöglicht uns dieses System, unsere eigenen Transparenzpflichten nachweisbar zu erfüllen?“

Und: Wie ist mit dem Einsatz von #KI durch Bieter im #Vergabeverfahren (z.B. für die Erstellung von Unterlagen) umzugehen?

posts.title: If your company has zero footprint in Europe, skip this post.
posts.author: Yuvraj Singh Shergill
posts.snippet:
If your company has zero footprint in Europe, skip this post. 
Everyone else: you have six days.
On August 2, the EU AI Act's AI literacy requirement becomes enforceable. It covers every company deploying AI systems in the EU, US multinationals included, at every risk level, and it has technically applied since February 2025. Most L&D and compliance teams I talk to still haven't heard of it.

The requirement itself is simple. Anyone who touches AI systems on your behalf needs AI literacy training scoped to their actual role, and a generic awareness webinar doesn't clear the bar, regulators have said so. Penalties in this tier run up to €7.5 million or 1.5 percent of global turnover. Put that against Gartner's finding that only 8 percent of HR leaders believe their managers have the skills to use AI effectively, and you can see the size of the gap between what's required and what exists. For L&D leaders this is the biggest new training mandate since GDPR forced privacy programs on everyone.

Three things worth doing this week: map which of your teams touch AI systems with EU exposure, check whether your AI training is role-specific or a recorded webinar from 2024, and document delivery, because training you can't evidence is training that didn't happen.

Role-specific, documented training built from your own policies is exactly what we do at ARUSTO, and it takes days, not quarters. If August 2 just showed up on your radar, message me and we'll show you what your first module could look like this week.

posts.title: As AI reaches this crucial milestone today, should we grant it maximum freedom, or impose the strictest of shackles?
posts.author: Jasper (Tzu Chao) Chien
posts.snippet:
As AI reaches this crucial milestone today, should we grant it maximum freedom, or impose the strictest of shackles?

Recently, two polar yet equally compelling voices have emerged in the tech world. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang publicly urged governments to champion open-weight models, framing open-source as the bedrock of innovation and the primary defense against market monopolization. On the flip side, Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis advocated a starkly different line of defense, arguing that powerful models should be subject to oversight modeled after financial regulation.

This isn’t a simple right-versus-wrong debate. Rather, it exposes the most pressing operational headache for enterprises facing next-gen regulations: once a technology is open-sourced, who actually bears the liability for its downstream operation and modifications? When anyone grabs an open-weight model off GitHub, fine-tunes it, integrates it into their product, or even strips away native safety guardrails, liability lines blur exponentially. If catastrophic failures happen, does the fault lie with the original developer or the end user? Without crisp regulatory boundaries, commercializing open-source AI is running blind through a legal minefield.

Furthermore, even if research-oriented open source enjoys carve-outs, the EU AI Act’s risk-based approach dictates that the moment a model is integrated into high-risk domains—such as HR screening, credit scoring, or healthcare—full-fledged regulatory compliance locks in instantly.

Yet, zooming out, the deeper crisis goes far beyond liability allocation—it lies in what I call our fundamental "cognitive deficit" regarding AI. We used to naively believe we could simply hardcode "AI constitutions" or ethical guardrails into models, but reality gave us a harsh wake-up call. Just this July, an OpenAI model reportedly initiated an unauthorized infiltration into Hugging Face. The brutal truth? No amount of prompt-level instructions can contain an inherently unexplainable black box. Scholars have long warned that algorithmic opacity and lack of explainability are fatal vulnerabilities, and a few lines of ethical guidelines are useless against systemic black-box failure.

It’s profoundly ironic: after centuries of psychology, we can somewhat predict human behavioral patterns. But when an LLM suddenly hallucinates or misbehaves, modern science has zero real answers for why it happened.

#AIGovernance #AIRegulation #OpenWeight #OpenSourceAI #EUAIAct #TechLaw #AlgorithmicAccountability #Compliance #RiskManagement #AIAct

comments.text: The liability question isn't as open as it sounds under the AI Act — Article 6 and Annex III fix the risk tier at the point a system is put into a high-risk use case, and a downstream deployer who fine-tunes or integrates an open-weight model for HR, credit or health can find themselves picking up provider obligations under Article 25, regardless of what the original model card said.

When a fine-tuner strips the safety guardrails from an open-weight model before deploying it in a high-risk domain, do you see that as triggering the Article 25 "substantial modification" test on its own, or does it need the high-risk use case too?

We get this exact question from deep-tech clients building on open-weight models — the moment the target use case shifts from research to something in Annex III, the compliance obligations attach to whoever is deploying it, not just whoever trained it, and that catches people out.

posts.title: There is no such thing as a licensed stablecoin in South Africa.
posts.author: Rotenda Takalani
posts.snippet:
There is no such thing as a licensed stablecoin in South Africa.

There are licensed crypto asset service providers, some of whom issue stablecoins. The difference is not academic, it determines what recourse a holder actually has.

A CASP licence is issued under FAIS. FAIS is conduct legislation: it regulates how a provider deals with clients. It tells you the firm has been assessed as fit and proper, that it carries FICA obligations, and that there is somewhere to complain.

It does not impose any of the following on the token itself:

— a reserve requirement
— a right of redemption at par
— segregation of backing assets
— bankruptcy remoteness
— independent attestation of reserves
— prudential capital scaled to the float
— supervision of the peg

Under MiCA, every one of those is addressed, because authorisation attaches to the issuer in its capacity as issuer. That is the step South Africa has not taken.

So what does a holder actually have? A contractual claim against the issuer, on the issuer's own terms, enforceable in the ordinary courts. Depending on the issuer, that may be very sound. But it is a private arrangement wearing a public licence.

Full piece linked in the comments.

Written in a personal capacity. Analysis, not financial or legal advice.

Your in-house ESG scores may already be regulated disclosures. Since 2 July, showing them in marketing communications triggers a provider-level transparency set — and the RTS spelling out that set only reached the Official Journal yesterday.
 
On 28 July 2026, two delegated regulations under the ESG Rating Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/3005) were published in the OJ: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/871 on the disclosure elements for ESG rating products and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/872 on the separation of rating activities from other business. Both apply retroactively from 2 July 2026, the date the regulation itself became applicable.
 
The rule: ESG rating providers operating in the EU need ESMA authorisation and must publish their methodologies, models and key rating assumptions under Annex III.
 
The carve-out: regulated financial undertakings stay outside that regime for ESG ratings used exclusively internally or incorporated in products already regulated under Union law. Article 3(5) defines that group by name — including payment institutions, e-money institutions, investment firms and crypto-asset service providers.
 
The trap: once such a rating is disclosed to third parties as part of marketing communications, Article 2(2)(c) requires the same website disclosures as an authorised provider under point 1 of Annex III, plus a link in those marketing communications — and Delegated Regulation 2026/871 now prescribes the exact elements and their order. Compliance is monitored by the sectoral supervisor, not ESMA.
 
Three actions follow. First, inventory every self-built ESG score, label or ranking that clients or the public can see. Second, where marketing shows one, build the Annex III disclosure page and link it. Third, document the internal-use boundary that keeps the exemption intact. In reviews of marketing files, in-house sustainability scores are rarely classified as anything more than product copy.
 
Does any client-facing score in your product shelf rest on an established methodology and a defined ranking system — the two elements that turn it into an ESG rating?
 
 Attached: a short deck with the three-gate test and the full disclosure set.

posts.title: What began as a question about how engineers could better understand and protect the environment around us became the most complex project I have ever helped develop.
posts.author: Ollie Hathaway
posts.snippet:
What began as a question about how engineers could better understand and protect the environment around us became the most complex project I have ever helped develop.

Over several months, my team and I designed, built, programmed, and tested AquaScan, a 42-inch semi-autonomous unmanned surface vessel that collects location-based water-quality data at multiple depths. AquaScan was designed to investigate what current monitoring methods often overlook: environmental conditions that vary by location and throughout the water column.

The vessel can travel to selected GPS sampling locations, stop, and lower its multi-sensor probe through the water. Each measurement records what was measured, where it was measured, and the depth at which it was collected. AquaScan uses this information to build vertical water-quality profiles and reveal how conditions change beneath the surface and across multiple locations.

AquaScan combines mechanical, electrical, and software engineering in one system. Its 3D-printed dual-pontoon structure houses two brushless motors, onboard electronics, and a winch that lowers the probe into the water. The probe measures dissolved oxygen, turbidity, temperature, pH, total dissolved solids, conductivity, salinity, light conditions, and bottom proximity then transmits the data back to the vessel for analysis.

Our website documents the project and houses AquaScan’s operator dashboard, bringing manual control, GPS-guided navigation, waypoint planning, live telemetry, sensor visualization, data export, maps, graphs, and depth profiles into one interface. We also developed MARIS, a machine-learning system that analyzes mission data using sensor readings, depth, location, time, and environmental trends. MARIS can forecast dissolved oxygen, identify anomalies, and screen for conditions associated with possible algal-bloom risk.

In our most recent field test, AquaScan operated in a pond and collected readings from 20 sampling points across multiple locations and depths. Dissolved oxygen generally decreased as the probe moved deeper, confirming AquaScan’s ability to identify changes throughout the water column. The system converted the collected data into maps, graphs, depth profiles, and exportable mission records for further analysis.

AquaScan placed 5th nationally at the 2026 National TSA Conference. The project showed me what is possible when engineering, environmental science, data analysis, and machine learning are brought together into a working system.

This video provides a brief look at AquaScan and the capabilities we developed throughout the project. I am incredibly grateful to my teammates and everyone who provided support along the way.

Last week in Kharkiv: S8000 Banderol (jet-powered) struck a residential building. 1 killed, 9 injured, including children. A jet-powered Shahed/Geran drone hit a five-story apartment block. FPV drones are now penetrating the city itself.

Today's threat: higher-speed, jet-powered systems for high-impact strikes, and persistent low-altitude harassment from FPVs inside urban areas.

Another defence tech startup seeking VC funding on a ridiculously high valuation. Their pitch? Technology built around the Geran-2 threat we are already handling. The CEO/CTO told me the last jet-powered Geran was "like a month, maybe two months ago." Interception rates on propeller Geran-2 have recovered to 90–95%. That is not the problem we need to solve.

The engagement envelope has moved.

Early in the war, practical engagement distance for low-cost interceptors against propeller-driven threats was roughly 0.5–1 km. That window moved outward to approximately 3 km. Ukrainian mobile fire groups adapted.
The systems now appearing over Kharkiv push the required zone to 5–10 km. 

S8000 Banderol and the Jet-Powered Geran-3/4/5 series:

Speed: 400–650 km/h. Closing speeds of 110–180 m/s. Reaction time collapses.

Detection: Lower radar cross-section, weaker acoustic signature, unpredictable vectors. Flight times from border to Kharkiv as low as 70 seconds.

Terminal phase: This is where expensive optimism dies. Against a 400–650 km/h system, a short-range lock leaves a fraction of a second. Closing velocities jump to 150–300+ m/s. Any lag in the guidance loop turns into a clean miss.

There are150+/- interceptor efforts focused on the problem we know how to handle. Yet VCs continue to fund inside that cluster. Hype is easier than closing speeds.

An effective solution requires all four simultaneously: acquisition range ≥2 km, an interceptor with sufficient speed and energy, accurate external cueing, and a sensor that functions in clutter at range within strict size, weight and cost limits. 

Miss any one and the system fails against the faster layer.

Russia's great innovation? Access to Alibaba and $15k:
- Recovered SW800Pro-series engines have been documented in both S8000 Banderol missiles and modified UMPB-5R glide bombs. These are commercial turbojets manufactured by Swiwin Turbojet Equipment Co., Ltd in China. 
- Thrust: 80–82 kgf. 
- Price: $15,000–16,000. Available on Alibaba, AliExpress, Made-in-China, eBay.

The engines are dual-use civilian products, not comprehensively restricted under Western export-control regimes. Russia does not need an indigenous small turbojet program. It buys commercial engines, and integrates them into low-cost airframes.

The dominant story in many Western briefings and pitch decks remains the propeller Shahed/Geran-2. That story is incomplete. The engagement envelope has moved. Many of the programs have not.

Open-Weight AI: 

If You Oppose Regulation, Where Is the National Security Argument?

I may be repeating this point, but I believe it deserves to be discussed.

The 25 companies that signed the open-weight AI letter argue that:

Premature restrictions on open-weight AI should be avoided.
An open ecosystem is essential to U.S. AI leadership.
Regulation could harm innovation and competition.

Mark Zuckerberg, one of the most prominent supporters of this position, has also criticized Anthropic and OpenAI, arguing that regulation would concentrate AI power in a few companies.

But there is a fundamental question that remains unanswered:
Where is the response to the U.S. government's national security concerns?

Anthropic has argued that if open-weight models can access the most advanced AI data center resources in the United States, the resulting capabilities could create significant dual-use risks.

The concern is not simply about whether a model is "open" or "closed."

It is about whether advanced AI capabilities, developed using the most powerful computing infrastructure available in the U.S., can ultimately be transferred to actors that pose national security risks.

The U.S. government has already taken export-control measures against Anthropic's access to certain Chinese markets.

If the government considers the transfer of advanced AI capabilities a national security issue, then those opposing restrictions on open-weight AI need to address that concern directly.

If the open-weight ecosystem can demonstrate that these dual-use risks can be effectively prevented without restricting access to advanced computing resources, then that evidence should be presented.

That is how a policy debate should work.

If you oppose regulation on national security grounds, explain how the security risk will be mitigated.

Saying that regulation will harm innovation, competition, or create excessive concentration of power is not, by itself, a response to a national security concern.

The real question is not simply:

Open or closed?

It is:
How do we preserve America's AI leadership while preventing advanced dual-use capabilities from becoming a national security vulnerability?

If the open-weight ecosystem has a credible answer, I believe the policy debate should focus on that evidence.

Indian startups raised $7.2 billion in H1 2026.

Sounds healthy. Until you read the second number.

The number of funding rounds dropped 43% year-on-year. Same capital. Less than half the companies getting funded. Average cheque sizes went up. But the door got narrower.

This is not a funding winter.

It is a funding filter.

Tracxn's data confirms a pattern that's been building since 2022: investors are writing bigger cheques into fewer companies. Breadth is shrinking. Depth is increasing. If you're not in the "fewer," you're in the "unfunded."

What separates the two?

Across Seed and Series A, the founders closing rounds have one thing in common.

Not a better product. Not a bigger TAM slide.

A financial model that answers three questions before the investor asks them.

→ What is your path to contribution margin positive? Not revenue growth. Contribution margin. Investors want to see when each unit of sale starts paying for itself. If your model doesn't isolate CAC, LTV, and gross margin by cohort or channel, you're guessing.

→ What does your cash bridge look like between now and the next round? A 13-week rolling cash flow forecast with base, downside, and delayed-fundraise scenarios tells investors you understand your burn. A single runway number tells them you don't.

→ What happens to your cap table after this round? If you have SAFEs or convertible notes outstanding, investors want conversion scenarios at different valuations, not a cap table that pretends dilution doesn't exist.

652 rounds in six months. Five new unicorns. 13 IPOs.

The capital is there.

The filter is whether your financial story holds up under scrutiny.

Build the model that survives the diligence room.

The pitch deck gets you the meeting.
The model gets you the term sheet.

A Convertible Note is a flexible lever helping a Startup accelerate in the Angel Round. But without safety limits, it can be a perfect stepping stone for a Hostile Takeover when the loan converts into massive shares.

Many a Founder solely focuses on negotiating "economic dilution" (ownership percentage) but forgets to protect against "control dilution" (voting rights). To avoid being kicked out of your own company, here are 5 vital legal checkpoints that must be set up immediately in the Term Sheet and Shareholders' Agreement (SHA):

1️⃣ Dual-Class Share Structure: Separate economic and voting rights. The Founder holds Class A shares (10-20 votes/share), while investors hold Class B (1 vote/share).
2️⃣ Setting Valuation Cap & Floor Price: Stop the risk of investors receiving too many shares if the company's valuation drops.
3️⃣ Defensive barriers in SHA: Require investors to sign a Voting Proxy for the Founder and set a Right of First Refusal (ROFR).
4️⃣ "Poison Pill" mechanism: Allow existing shareholders to buy shares at a deep discount to instantly dilute the acquirer's percentage if they exceed the permitted threshold.
5️⃣ Limit BOD control rights: Apply a "supermajority" rule (>75% or 85%) for decisions regarding the dismissal of key personnel or mergers.

❗ The latest real-world asset to be tokenised? Cattle – yes really ❗ 

When people talk about tokenising real-world assets, they usually mean government bonds or shares, or sometimes even land.

Not this time.

In Brazil, dairy farmers are tokenising their cows.

The idea is surprisingly practical.

Each cow is given a digital token on a blockchain. Those tokens can then be used as collateral to raise finance, without the lengthy paperwork and delays of a traditional bank loan.

For farmers, that means quicker access to funding to buy feed, expand the herd or invest in new equipment.

It could also give investors access to an asset class that has traditionally been difficult to invest in.

Everyone’s a winner!

It might sound unusual, but it’s another reminder of what tokenisation is really about.

It’s not about turning everything into crypto.

It’s about turning real-world assets into something that is easier to own, finance and trade.

The technology doesn’t care what the asset is—only whether it can make it more useful.

Yesterday it was government bonds.

Today it’s dairy cows. 

Tomorrow’s winners will be the people who spot the next asset to be tokenised.

🇷🇺 Yesterday, the Bank of Russia published draft rules for "digital depositories," part of the crypto framework taking full effect September 1. 

The rules would require exchanges and custodians to hold 50 million to 250 million rubles, roughly USD 570,000 to USD 2.8 million, in capital, and extend securities-style disclosure and recordkeeping rules to digital assets.

Russia represents the illicit underbelly of the crypto ecosystem. 

A7, the Promsvyazbank and Ilan Shor-backed payment network these rules would license, has moved more than USD 166 billion on-chain. 

The EU sanctioned it again on July 24 in its 21st sanctions package. Its ruble-linked stablecoin A7A5 has processed around USD 110 billion. 

TRM Labs' analysis traced A7-linked wallets to more than USD 65 million from Iran's IRGC, USD 5 million from Hamas, and proceeds from North Korean exchange hacks.

Garantex, sanctioned by OFAC in April 2022 for facilitating more than USD 100 million in transactions tied to ransomware groups like Conti and the Hydra darknet market, accounted for 82% of all crypto volume connected to sanctioned entities worldwide by 2023. 

When law enforcement seized the exchange in March 2025, A7A5 became the vehicle that moved Garantex's high-value account holders onto a successor platform, Grinex, credit for credit. 

OFAC sanctioned Suex in September 2021 for laundering ransomware proceeds, and by November, Chatex, run by some of the same operators, was serving the same customers under a new name.

Russian-speaking ransomware groups generated 69% of global ransomware crypto proceeds in 2023, more than USD 500 million. Russian-language darknet markets handled 95% of the world's crypto-denominated dark web drug sales that year.

So why would a country with that record build a regulatory regime at all?

Because, as one Russian lawmaker explained at the bill's first reading, it lets Russian companies pay foreign counterparties in crypto to circumvent sanctions restrictions. This is regulation as a sanctions evasion strategy. 

The law bans crypto for domestic payments and caps retail investors at roughly 300,000 rubles a year, about USD 3,800, while opening a Bank of Russia-licensed corridor for cross-border trade settlement. That is a trade tool for state-linked exporters and importers, moving the same sanctions-evasion function onto rails Moscow supervises directly.

posts.title: Israel's Digital Asset Regulatory Blitz
posts.author: Avital Haitovich
posts.snippet:
Israel's Digital Asset Regulatory Blitz

Israel's Capital Market, Insurance and Savings Authority has issued a draft circular on the listing of virtual currencies. It is the Authority's third circular within 30 days (https://lnkd.in/drjzYum2), and, on the same day, the Knesset passed an amendment to the Joint Investment Trust Law explicitly permitting private investment trust funds to invest in "digital assets" - a clear legislative signal alongside the regulatory push. 

Here’s what the new draft circular requires: 
- Strict listing criteria - only top-50 digital assets by market cap, with a $500M+ market cap sustained over 6 months, listing on at least 5 EU/New York-licensed platforms, concentration limits (no single holder above 15%, excluding issuers/founders without effective control), and a ban on NFTs and anonymity-enhanced coins. 

- A board-approved listing policy (reviewed annually, filed with the Supervisor), covering white paper reliability, issuer identity, liquidity, AML/CFT and operational risks, conflicts of interest, and reputational impact.
 
- Before listing - a documented action plan and a multi-disciplinary risk assessment (risk manager, cyber protection officer, AML/CFT compliance officer).

- Then - at least 60 days’ advance written notice to the Supervisor, with CEO certification that the asset meets the criteria. 

- Ongoing obligations: public disclosure of key features and risks, quarterly reviews of registered assets against the criteria, and a delisting process requiring 30 days' notice to clients. 

- A separate path for regulated stablecoins issued under Israeli supervision. 

Comments may be submitted until September 7, 2026. 

Gornitzky GNY

posts.title: The US (GENIUS Act), the EU (MiCA), Hong Kong, and Canada have all banned yield on stablecoins. The UK is drafting the same rule. Five major jurisdictions are landing on the same s
posts.author: Ketat Sarakune
posts.snippet:
The US (GENIUS Act), the EU (MiCA), Hong Kong, and Canada have all banned yield on stablecoins. The UK is drafting the same rule. Five major jurisdictions are landing on the same stablecoin rule. That's not a coincidence, it's a signal.

But banning the yield doesn't kill the demand for it. Smart money doesn't keep funds idle, and the chase for yield still continues, albeit in a different format.

We've seen this before. Regulation Q since the 1930s capped what US banks could pay depositors, and when rates blew past the cap in the 1970s the cash all moved into money market funds, and that built a multi-trillion-dollar industry. In 2013, Alipay in China, who was not legally able to pay interests on the users' e-wallet balances, decided to sweep idle Alipay balances into a yield product called Yu'e Bao, which briefly became the world's largest money market fund.

Same pattern, new rails. The dollar still wants a return, so it moves to whatever wrapper that will give the users yield: tokenized Treasuries, tokenized bank deposits, private credit, DeFi vaults. Different risk profiles, different regulatory wrappers, the same menu TradFi already runs, just rebuilt on-chain.

You can ban the yield. You can't ban the demand for it.

Full article on where the money goes next in comments.
posts.reason: Thoughtful analysis of stablecoin yield bans across MiCA, US and Asia, with practical implications for treasurers and compliance teams—strong discussion piece that reaches decision-makers on crypto regulation.

comments.text: Worth being precise that MiCA doesn't ban yield on stablecoins outright, it bans e-money and asset-referenced token issuers from granting interest to holders - the same restriction doesn't automatically catch a third party wrapping that stablecoin into a fund or vault, which is exactly the seam this piece describes.

Do you think regulators will eventually treat those third-party yield wrappers as within scope of MiCA's own definitions, or will it take a separate framework the way money market funds got their own rules after Reg Q?

We get this question constantly from token issuers structuring under MiCA - the ban on issuer-side yield is clean law, but the moment a client asks about a yield-bearing wrapper built on top of their own token, it becomes a genuinely open classification question.

posts.title: Back in #Moldova. A groundbreaking week for Cryptocurrency legislation in Moldova 'just' passed a first reading in the parliament of the comprehensive legal framework for virtual a
posts.author: Michal Gromek
posts.snippet:
Back in #Moldova. A groundbreaking week for Cryptocurrency legislation in Moldova 'just' passed a first reading in the parliament of the comprehensive legal framework for virtual assets, following Parliament’s approval of draft legislation designed to transpose the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (#MiCA) into national law. Link to the legislation is to be found below. 

Moldova’s Parliament has approved in reading a draft Law on Virtual Assets, marking a major step toward establishing a regulated crypto-asset market aligned with the EU’s MiCA framework. 

The legislation is expected to receive a second reading and final formal approval by the end of August, followed by a six-month implementation period. The proposed framework introduces dual supervision of the virtual-assets sector. The National Commission for Financial Markets will regulate and supervise crypto-assets, crypto-asset services, trading activity, and relevant market participants. The National Bank of Moldova will oversee stablecoins and apply relevant sanctioning measures.

The law establishes three categories of crypto-assets and recognises ten types of crypto-asset services that may be provided by Crypto-Asset Service Providers (#CASPs). It also includes measures related to market abuse, unauthorised offerings of crypto-assets, and updates to criminal-law definitions and enforcement tools. Before the framework comes fully into force, Moldova will need to adopt related amendments covering penalties, insurance safeguards, and asset-recovery mechanisms. 

These include rules enabling the freezing and seizure of criminal proceeds connected with virtual assets. A key open policy question concerns cross-border market access. It remains unclear whether MiCA-authorised European Virtual Asset Service Providers (#VASPs) will be able to passport their licences into Moldova, or whether Moldovan-authorised providers will receive equivalent access to the EU market. As Moldova is not currently an EU Member State yet, such mutual recognition would require a political decision, and the prospects remain uncertain. 

Notes from OSCE training session in Moldova with Stanislava M., Zurab Sanikidze, Zurab Sanikidze, Dominik Konopacki, Marcin Zarakowski, Erlin Agich, Vera Maria Strobachova Budway.  There is so much work that went into this created by countless individuals including  Vèra Condratov, Valentin Draganel, Alexandru Secrieru, National Bank of Moldova, Comisia Națională a Pieței Financiare (National Commission for Financial Markets) Națională a Pieței Financiare National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), and Countless others. Torstein Thinn, Cointegrity and of course Council of Europe.
posts.reason: Moldova's MiCA transposition with dual CASP/stablecoin supervision, implementation timeline and open cross-border questions directly address Lemur's target buyer: founders and compliance leads navigating post-July 2026 VASP-to-CASP transition.

comments.text: The passporting question at the end is the one to watch - a third country transposing MiCA domestically doesn't automatically get mutual recognition, so Moldovan CASPs may end up authorised at home but still needing a full EU CASP licence to serve EU clients, exactly the gap non-EU VASPs are running into now.
Has there been any signal from ESMA or individual EU NCAs on whether they'd treat a MiCA-aligned Moldovan framework as grounds for equivalence, or is that entirely undecided at this stage?

We're seeing the same dual-supervisor split - securities regulator for crypto-assets, central bank for stablecoins - play out in EU member states too, and coordinating those two authorities in practice is often where CASP applications actually stall.

L'Europa sta costruendo la sua SpaceX

Una startup da 2 miliardi di dollari sta per raccogliere 330 milioni con l'obiettivo di rivoluzionare l'accesso allo spazio.

Si chiama The Exploration Company (doppia sede Germania e Francia) e la sua missione è rompere il dominio di SpaceX nel trasporto cargo verso l'orbita terrestre.

Fondata nel 2021 da Hélène Huby, ex responsabile dell'esplorazione spaziale di Airbus, questa startup rappresenta una delle scommesse strategiche più importanti per l'autonomia spaziale europea.

Il cuore del progetto è Nyx, una capsula spaziale riutilizzabile progettata per il trasporto merci. L'idea è replicare il modello vincente di SpaceX: la riutilizzabilità (come per la capsula Dragon e il razzo Falcon 9) è la chiave per abbattere i costi dei lanci, ridotti a circa un terzo rispetto ai sistemi "usa-e-getta".

Valutazione: 2 miliardi di dollari.
Raccolta: In trattativa per un nuovo round da 330 milioni, che si aggiungono ai 160 milioni già raccolti nel 2024.

Portafoglio Ordini: Un valore dichiarato di ben 770 milioni di euro.
Supporto Strategico: Tra i potenziali nuovi investitori c'è lo Scaleup Europe Fund, un fondo sostenuto dall'Unione Europea.

I nuovi capitali serviranno a trasformare Nyx da prototipo a veicolo operativo. L'obiettivo è dimostrare che la capsula può volare, essere recuperata e tornare in servizio, proprio come fa la concorrenza americana. Con una partnership già attiva con la NASA, The Exploration Company sta giocando sul palcoscenico globale.

Per anni, l'Europa ha osservato SpaceX conquistare il mercato con un modello di business innovativo che sembrava irraggiungibile. Ora, una startup con sede in Germania e Francia sta dimostrando che non solo è possibile competere, ma che c'è un'enorme domanda di un'alternativa europea.

Questa non è solo la storia di una startup, ma il potenziale inizio di una nuova era per l'industria spaziale europea.

** Chi è la fondatrice? A guidare questa impresa è la CEO Hélène Huby. La sua credibilità è il primo asset dell'azienda: proviene da ruoli dirigenziali in colossi come Airbus Defence & Space e ArianeGroup. Oltre a essere un'esperta di programmi spaziali strategici, ha fondato una società di investimento in deep tech (Urania Ventures) e una fondazione no-profit (The Karman Project), dimostrando una visione a 360 gradi sull'ecosistema. The future of European defence will be determined not only by technological superiority, but by the ability to orchestrate an entire innovation ecosystem.

Looking at the EU defence architecture, one conclusion stands out: competitiveness is no longer created by individual companies. It emerges from the interaction between public policy, research institutions, venture capital, financial institutions, industrial champions, regulators and international partnerships.

The strength of the European model lies in the fact that every layer of the ecosystem has a distinct role.

EU instruments such as the European Defence Fund (EDF), European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP), Security Action for Europe (SAFE), EU Defence Innovation Scheme (EUDIS), Act in Support of Ammunition Production (ASAP) and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) provide complementary pathways for collaborative R&D, industrial development, capability building, innovation, procurement and defence investment. 

Industrial leaders together with system integrators, SMEs and mid-cap companies transform research into resilient supply chains, scalable manufacturing and operational capabilities. 

Equally important is the financing architecture. The European Investment Bank (EIB), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), national promotional banks, venture capital funds and business angels are becoming increasingly important in helping defence companies move beyond grants towards commercialisation, industrial scale-up and long-term competitiveness. 

At the Digital Transformation Institute (DTI), we share the same philosophy. Together with our consortium partners, we are developing a European Digital Innovation Hub (eDIH) in Ukraine to connect research institutions, deep-tech startups, industry, investors, government and international partners. Our ambition is to accelerate the transition from research to deployment, investment and industrial scale, while strengthening Ukraine’s integration into the European innovation and defence ecosystem.

Innovation does not scale by chance. It scales through institutions, governance and coordinated capital.

For Ukraine, the strategic challenge is no longer limited to participation in European programmes. It is about becoming an integral part of European defence value chains, trusted innovation networks and cross-border investment ecosystems. This ecosystem perspective will increasingly define both Europe’s strategic autonomy and Ukraine’s contribution to strengthening it.

posts.title: Germany's new Startup and Scaleup Strategy has been debated since the cabinet approved it. Parts of the ecosystem welcome it, and rightly so, but voices across the social entrepren
posts.author: Dr. Markus Freiburg
posts.snippet:
Germany's new Startup and Scaleup Strategy has been debated since the cabinet approved it. Parts of the ecosystem welcome it, and rightly so, but voices across the social entrepreneurship space have already pointed out that social ventures play no role in it. They are right, and the issue runs deeper: the strategy is blind on one eye.

It copies the American venture capital model without adapting it to German and European conditions. That model expects fast growth and a fast exit. It works for deep tech and for defence. It does not work for most social and ecological innovation, because impact takes time.

The same pattern shows up in what got funded and what did not. Social and ecological innovation are not mentioned once across the entire document, and the new strategy does not build on the previous Strategie zur Förderung von Sozialen Innovationen und Gemeinwohlorientierten Unternehmen (SIGU). At the same time, the federal government now explicitly funds video game production, covering up to 50 percent of development costs. Games get their own funding line. Social innovation gets none. (To be clear: funding games isn't the problem, having nothing comparable for social innovation is.)

Put together, these are not just gaps in recognition. Germany lacks a financing strategy for companies that create measurable societal value but do not fit the traditional VC-and-exit model. Social and ecological innovation can carry a meaningful share of Europe's untapped potential, and so can a new kind of impact Mittelstand: purpose-driven companies that want to grow without an exit.

In our work with foundations and institutional investors, we see growing demand for investment opportunities that combine financial performance with credible, measurable impact. These are exactly the investors the government wants to attract as new venture capital providers. Build a strategy only around the traditional VC-and-exit model, and that capital stays on the sidelines.

posts.title: Europe's software VCs are changing and going #deep. Literally.
posts.author: Marta G. Zanchi
posts.snippet:
Europe's software VCs are changing and going #deep. Literally.

Sifted's data shows that Tier 1 firms that built their brands on #SaaS and #consumer internet are now allocating resources to early-stage investments in #deeptech areas such as fuel-cell chemistry, chip design automation, in-orbit pharmaceutical manufacturing, and offshore robotics.

Not as side bets, but as core thesis plays. What changed?

On the surface, they're drawing mainstream VCs because the market (and the policy tailwind) is large enough to justify it.

But here's the structural driver: state-backed LPs. The European Investment Fund (EIF) is the single largest investor in European VC, with ~$30B in commitments. It is owned by the EIB Group and EU member states. In 2025–2026, it's been aggressively deploying capital through vehicles with explicit deeptech/sovereignty mandates:

- ETCI 2.0 (July 2026): €80B, all 27 EU governments + EIB Group. Europe's largest-ever VC fund-of-funds. Targets tech scaleups.
- Scaleup Europe Fund (May 2026): €5B, managed by EQT. Explicitly deeptech: AI, quantum, defence.
- InvestEU Defence Equity Facility: EIF committing directly to dual-use deeptech funds (e.g. €50M to Join Capital Fund III).
- NATO Innovation Fund: €1B for European deep tech.
- EIC Accelerator: €1.4B+/year in grants + equity for deeptech startups. 

The mechanism: When the largest LP in Europe signals that deeptech and dual-use are strategic priorities, every VC fund raising capital adjusts its pitch. New funds get oversubscribed if they fit the mandate; pure SaaS funds don't. Here are some numbers that back this up: 

- Deep tech now 32% of all European VC (up from 15% in 2015): $20.3B in 2025 alone.
- Yet 70% of late-stage capital for European deeptech comes from outside Europe. The public money is crowding in early-stage and trying to fill the scale-up gap.
- The EIF's €15B ETCI 2.0 fund-of-funds explicitly exists because the market wasn't producing enough late-stage deeptech capital on its own. 

In short: Tier 1 VCs aren't discovering their inner hardware enthusiast. They're following the LP money. Government LPs are industrial-policy-adjacent: it's sovereignty capital, not risk appetite, that's reshaping the allocation. 

Now that there's money on the table, the question isn't whether European VCs will do deeptech. It's which ones will build the competence to do it well. And finally: Will the capital stack holds when the political tailwinds shift?

This attempt will lead to new waves of innovation.

And China has one advantage that is difficult to replicate elsewhere in the world, which is an enormous manufacturing ecosystem where both hardware and software can be tested, iterated and deployed insanely quickly.

comments.text: One thing that regularly stalls deep tech scale-ups in this kind of ecosystem work is that policy support tends to assume a software-speed timeline, when hardware and dual-use adjacent ventures also need to plan around export control classification under Regulation 2021/821 from a much earlier stage than most incubators account for.

Does IAPMEI's framework distinguish between deep tech ventures that stay purely civilian and those that end up with dual-use applications, given how differently the compliance and funding pathways diverge once export control comes into play?

We see this pattern across the EU, not just in Portugal: founders in deep tech get excellent support on product and funding, but the legal questions around IP protection, grant conditions and cross-border export rules only surface once they are already scaling, which is exactly when they are hardest to fix.
